asset_pages.title: Bank FD & Deposits After Death — Nominee, ₹15 Lakh Threshold & Succession Certificate
asset_pages.desc: What happens to a bank account or FD when the holder dies: when a nominee means no succession certificate is needed, the ₹15 lakh simplified-procedure threshold, and the 15-day settlement rule (RBI Directions, 2025).
asset_pages.lede: Bank deposits are the most common reason families need a succession certificate — but since the RBI's 2025 Directions, many bank claims do not need one at all. It depends on whether there is a nominee and how much is involved.

sections.h: If there is a nominee — no succession certificate, whatever the amount
sections.p: Under the RBI (Settlement of Claims in respect of Deceased Customers of Banks) Directions, 2025 (26 September 2025), where there is a nominee or a survivorship clause, the bank must NOT insist on a succession certificate, probate, letters of administration, an indemnity bond or a surety — whatever the amount. The nominee needs only the claim form, the death certificate and ID/address proof. The nominee receives the money as a trustee for the legal heirs, not as the owner.

sections.h: If there is no nominee — below the threshold (₹15 lakh / ₹5 lakh)
sections.p: The threshold limit is ₹15 lakh for commercial and other banks and ₹5 lakh for co-operative banks (a bank may fix a higher limit). Below the threshold, the simplified procedure applies and no succession certificate is needed: claim form, death certificate, ID/address proof of the claimants, an indemnity bond (no third-party surety may be insisted on within the threshold), a no-objection from the non-claiming heirs, and proof of heirship via a legal-heir certificate or a declaration by an independent person known to the family. Conditions: no will, no contesting claim, and no court order restraining payment.

sections.h: If there is no nominee — above the threshold
sections.p: Above the threshold, the bank may settle on a succession certificate, OR a legal-heir certificate, OR a sworn affidavit (before a magistrate / judicial authority) — and it may seek a surety. Older guides say a succession certificate is 'the normal requirement' above the threshold; the 2025 Directions list it as one of three options, so do not treat it as mandatory — ask the bank which of the three it accepts.

sections.h: How fast must the bank settle
sections.p: The bank must settle a deposit claim within 15 calendar days of receiving all the required documents. Delay attracts interest of at least the Bank Rate + 4% per year for the delay period. The Directions were to be implemented by banks no later than 31 March 2026 — if your bank is still following an older process, point it at the 2025 Directions.

asset_pages.certificate: No will + no nominee + above ₹15 lakh: a succession certificate is the most widely accepted of the three options the bank may accept. Below the threshold, or with a nominee, you usually do not need one at all. Use the wizard to check your situation, and the petition draft if a succession certificate is the route.

faq.q: Do I need a succession certificate if there is a nominee?
faq.a: No. Under the RBI Directions, 2025, where there is a nominee or a survivorship clause, the bank must not insist on a succession certificate, probate, letters of administration, an indemnity bond or a surety — whatever the amount. The nominee only needs the claim form, the death certificate and ID/address proof.

faq.q: What is the ₹15 lakh threshold?
faq.a: Below ₹15 lakh (commercial and other banks) or ₹5 lakh (co-operative banks), and with no nominee, the bank uses a simplified procedure — claim form, death certificate, ID/address proof, an indemnity bond and an NOC from the non-claiming heirs. No succession certificate is needed below the threshold.

faq.q: The bank is asking for a succession certificate above ₹15 lakh — is it mandatory?
faq.a: Not under the 2025 Directions: above the threshold the bank may settle on a succession certificate, OR a legal-heir certificate, OR a sworn affidavit before a magistrate / judicial authority. A succession certificate is one of three options — ask the bank which it accepts.

faq.q: How long should the bank take?
faq.a: 15 calendar days from receiving all the required documents. Delay attracts interest of at least the Bank Rate + 4% per year for the delay period.

asset_pages.title: Shares & Demat After Death — Transmission, Nominee & SEBI Value Tiers
asset_pages.desc: How shares and mutual fund units pass to the heirs: transmission (not transfer), the nominee as trustee, and SEBI's value tiers — up to ₹30,000, up to ₹30 lakh, and above ₹30 lakh (SEBI circular, 23 July 2026).
asset_pages.lede: Shares and Demat holdings pass by transmission after death — not by transfer. Whether you need a succession certificate depends on whether there is a nominee and on the value involved.

sections.p: With a nominee, the nominee receives the securities as a trustee on behalf of the legal heir(s) — no succession certificate is needed. The documents are the transmission request form (TRF), the death certificate, the client master report and KYC. The nominee is a trustee, not the owner: the value belongs to the legal heirs under succession law.

sections.h: If there is a joint holder
sections.p: On the death of one joint holder, the surviving holder takes the securities by survivorship on the death certificate alone.

sections.h: If there is no nominee — SEBI value tiers (Demat)
sections.p: Up to ₹30,000: Quick Transmission Processing — a plain-paper request plus proof of relationship (immediate relatives only). Up to ₹30 lakh: simplified procedure — a notarised indemnity bond plus an affidavit-cum-NOC from all the heirs, or a family settlement deed. Above ₹30 lakh: an affidavit-cum-NOC plus one of — a will (with indemnity), a legal-heirship certificate (Tahsildar rank or above, with indemnity), or a succession certificate / letter of administration / court decree. For physical shares the tiers are ₹10,000 and ₹10 lakh. Probate of a will is no longer a mandatory requirement.
Entities should ordinarily complete transmission within 21 calendar days of receiving all the documents, giving written reasons for any delay or rejection.

asset_pages.certificate: No nominee + Demat holdings above ₹30 lakh: a succession certificate is one of three documents the depository may accept (the others are a will with indemnity, or a legal-heirship certificate with indemnity). Below ₹30 lakh, the simplified procedure applies and no succession certificate is needed. With a nominee, none is needed at any value.

faq.q: Do I need a succession certificate for shares if there is a nominee?
faq.a: No. With a nominee, the securities are transmitted to the nominee as a trustee for the legal heirs, on the transmission request form, the death certificate, the client master report and KYC. No succession certificate is needed.

faq.q: What are SEBI's value tiers for transmission without a nominee?
faq.a: For Demat holdings: up to ₹30,000 is Quick Transmission Processing; up to ₹30 lakh needs a notarised indemnity bond plus an affidavit-cum-NOC from all heirs (or a family settlement deed); above ₹30 lakh needs an affidavit-cum-NOC plus one of a will, a legal-heirship certificate, or a succession certificate / letter of administration / court decree. Physical shares use ₹10,000 and ₹10 lakh tiers.

faq.q: Is the nominee the owner of the shares?
faq.a: No. The nominee receives the securities as a trustee on behalf of the legal heir(s). The value belongs to the heirs under succession law.

faq.q: How long does transmission take?
faq.a: Ordinarily within 21 calendar days of receiving all the documents, with written reasons for any delay or rejection.

asset_pages.title: EPF After Death — Form 20, Pension (Form 10D) & EDLI (Form 5IF)
asset_pages.desc: What the family of a deceased EPF member can claim: final settlement (Form 20), monthly pension (Form 10D), withdrawal benefit (Form 10C) and EDLI insurance up to ₹7 lakh (Form 5IF).
asset_pages.lede: A deceased EPF member's family can claim the PF balance, a monthly pension and an insurance amount — each on a different form. None of these needs a succession certificate: they are claimed through the EPFO on the member's nomination or heirship.

sections.h: Form 20 — final settlement of the PF balance
sections.p: Form 20 is for the final EPF settlement by the nominee or the legal heir of a deceased member. It is submitted via the last employer to the EPFO (also online via EPFO death-claim filing). The death certificate and cancelled cheque / bank details are required.
Form 10D claims the monthly pension under the Employees' Pension Scheme — widow / widower pension, children pension and orphan pension.
Form 10C is for the withdrawal benefit where the member died after age 58 with less than 10 years of service.

Form 5IF claims the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance (EDLI) where the member died while in service. EDLI is automatic for EPF members and is funded by the employer (0.5% of wages, capped at ₹75 a month) — there is no separate enrolment and no employee contribution. The maximum benefit is ₹7 lakh (35 times the average monthly wage of the last 12 months, wage capped at ₹15,000, plus a bonus of up to ₹1.75 lakh linked to the average PF balance). The minimum is ₹2.5 lakh (12+ months' service); since the 18 July 2025 amendment, the minimum is ₹50,000 where the average PF balance is below ₹50,000 or the member died before completing a year.

asset_pages.certificate: EPF claims are made on the EPFO's own forms (20 / 10D / 10C / 5IF) through the nominee or the legal heir — a succession certificate is not the route for PF money. If the EPFO asks for proof of heirship, a legal-heir certificate is the usual document.

faq.q: Which form claims the PF balance of a deceased member?
faq.a: Form 20 — final settlement by the nominee or the legal heir, submitted via the last employer to the EPFO (also online). The death certificate and bank details are required.

faq.q: What is EDLI and how much does it pay?
faq.a: EDLI (Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance) is automatic life cover for EPF members who die while in service, claimed on Form 5IF. The maximum is ₹7 lakh; the minimum is ₹2.5 lakh (12+ months' service), or ₹50,000 after the 18 July 2025 amendment where the average PF balance is below ₹50,000.

faq.q: Does the family get a monthly pension?
faq.a: Yes, on Form 10D — widow / widower pension, children pension and orphan pension under the Employees' Pension Scheme.

faq.q: Do I need a succession certificate for EPF?
faq.a: No. EPF claims are made on the EPFO's own forms through the nominee or the legal heir. A legal-heir certificate is the usual proof of heirship if the EPFO asks for one.

asset_pages.title: Insurance Claim After Death — Nominee vs Legal Heir
asset_pages.desc: Who actually gets the insurance money: the nominee is a trustee, not the owner (Supreme Court, Sarbati Devi, 1984) — and the 'beneficial nominee' exception under Section 39(7) is still unsettled law.
asset_pages.lede: The person named as nominee on a life insurance policy is not necessarily the person who keeps the money. Under Indian law, the nominee is usually only a trustee for the legal heirs.

sections.h: The nominee is a trustee, not the owner
sections.p: The Supreme Court held in Sarbati Devi v. Usha Devi (1984) 1 SCC 424 that nomination under Section 39 of the Insurance Act, 1938 does not confer a beneficial interest: the nominee is only authorised to receive the amount, which forms part of the estate for distribution under succession law. This was reaffirmed in later cases, including Shakti Yezdani v. Jayanand Salgaonkar (2023). So the insurer pays the nominee, but the nominee holds the money in trust for the legal heirs.

The Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 introduced Section 39(7): where the nominee is the policyholder's spouse, parent or child, the nominee is a 'beneficial nominee' entitled to retain the proceeds as beneficial owner (unless it is shown the policyholder could not validly confer that). Nominees who are anyone else hold as trustees. BUT High Courts have diverged on this (for example Allahabad High Court, Kusum v. Anand Kumar, 2025) and the Supreme Court has not conclusively settled it. We flag this as unsettled — do not treat it as a firm rule.

Claim from the insurer with the death certificate and the policy details. If there is a dispute between the nominee and the other legal heirs about who keeps the money, that dispute is decided under succession law — and a succession certificate is the document that authorises the heirs to collect it.

asset_pages.certificate: If the insurer pays the nominee, the nominee holds the money in trust for the legal heirs. If the heirs need to collect the amount themselves — for example where there is no nominee, or the nominee has also died — a succession certificate from the District Court is the usual route.

faq.q: Is the insurance nominee the owner of the money?
faq.a: Usually no. The Supreme Court (Sarbati Devi v. Usha Devi, 1984) held that the nominee is only authorised to receive the amount; it forms part of the estate and belongs to the legal heirs under succession law.

faq.q: What is a 'beneficial nominee' under Section 39(7)?
faq.a: Since the 2015 amendment, a nominee who is the policyholder's spouse, parent or child is a 'beneficial nominee' entitled to retain the proceeds. But High Courts have diverged and the Supreme Court has not conclusively settled it — treat it as unsettled law, not a firm rule.

faq.q: There is no nominee on the policy — what then?
faq.a: The legal heirs claim from the insurer, and the insurer will usually ask for a succession certificate (or a legal-heir certificate) before paying.

asset_pages.title: Property After Death — Why a Succession Certificate Does Not Transfer Title
asset_pages.desc: A succession certificate covers debts and securities only — it does not move a house or land into your name (Supreme Court, Madhvi Amma, 2000). Property passes under personal law or the will, with mutation.
asset_pages.lede: The most common misunderstanding in this whole area: a succession certificate does not transfer a house or a plot of land. It covers debts and securities only.

sections.h: A succession certificate does not confer title
sections.p: The Supreme Court held in Madhvi Amma Bhawani Amma v. Kunjikutty Pillai Meenakshi Pillai (2000) 6 SCC 301: 'The grant of a succession certificate does not confer any title to the property of the deceased. It merely authorizes the holder to collect the debts and securities.' It does not move a flat, a plot or a house into your name.

Immovable property passes under personal law (or under the will, if there is one), and the heirs' names are then entered in the property records by mutation. A legal-heir certificate is likewise not proof of ownership — it identifies the heirs; it does not prove title.

If all the heirs agree on how the property is divided, a family settlement deed can record it without a court case. It must be voluntary, signed by all the members, with witnesses. If it creates, declares or extinguishes rights in immovable property in the present, it must be compulsorily registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (a mere memorandum recording a prior oral settlement need not be). Supreme Court: Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation.

asset_pages.certificate: For immovable property, the route is: establish who the heirs are (legal-heir certificate where issued, or probate if there is a will), then apply for mutation of the property records. A succession certificate is the wrong document for property — use the wizard to check, and do not pay a court fee for a certificate that cannot transfer title.

faq.q: Can I transfer a house with a succession certificate?
faq.a: No. A succession certificate covers debts and securities only. The Supreme Court (Madhvi Amma, 2000) held it 'does not confer any title to the property of the deceased. It merely authorizes the holder to collect the debts and securities.'

faq.q: How does property pass to the heirs then?
faq.a: Under personal law (or the will, if there is one), and the heirs' names are entered in the property records by mutation. A legal-heir certificate identifies the heirs but is not proof of ownership.

faq.q: All heirs agree on the division — do we need a court?
faq.a: Not necessarily: a family settlement deed can record the division without a court case, signed by all the heirs with witnesses. But if it deals with immovable property rights, it must be registered under the Registration Act, 1908.

succession: Identity proof of the applicant and all other heirs (Aadhaar / PAN)
Address proof of the applicant and all other heirs
Schedule of the debts and securities claimed, with values — the court fee is charged on this schedule, not on the whole estate
No-objection (NOC) statements / affidavits from the other legal heirs
Proof of relationship to the deceased
legal_heir: Identity proof of the applicant and all heirs
Ration card / family register showing all family members
Proof of relationship to the deceased
Affidavit / joint affidavit from all heirs (where the state asks for one)

legal_heir_states.authority: Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM), Revenue Dept, NCT of Delhi
legal_heir_states.notes: Delhi does not issue a document called a 'legal-heir certificate'. What it issues is a Surviving Member Certificate (SMC) — that is what Delhi offices and banks mean by a legal-heir certificate.

legal_heir_states.instead: Maharashtra has no notified 'legal-heir certificate' service. The equivalent is an heirship certificate under Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827, applied for in the civil court (City Civil Court / Bombay High Court original side, by value). The Maharashtra Court-Fees Act Sch.I Art.12 charges it at the probate rate on the property certified. For debts and securities, use a succession certificate from the District Court instead.

state_pages.title: Legal Heir Certificate in Tamil Nadu (Varisu) — Portal, Documents, Fee & Timeline
state_pages.desc: How to get a legal-heir (Varisu) certificate in Tamil Nadu: Tahsildar, TN e-Sevai service REV-114, ₹60 fee, 15–30 days, and the documents you need.
state_pages.lede: In Tamil Nadu the legal-heir certificate is called the Varisu certificate. It is issued by the Tahsildar (Taluk office) after a Village Administrative Officer / Revenue Inspector enquiry, through the TN e-Sevai portal.

sections.p: Apply on TN e-Sevai (service code REV-114) or at the Taluk office. The application must include ALL the legal heirs — leaving one out can cause rejection.
The e-Sevai service charge is ₹60. The certificate is typically issued in 15–30 days (official guidance says about 2 weeks in some guides).

faq.q: What is the Varisu certificate?
faq.a: The Varisu certificate is Tamil Nadu's legal-heir certificate. It identifies who the legal heirs of a deceased person are, and is used for government pension, gratuity and dues.

faq.q: Who issues it?
faq.a: The Tahsildar (Taluk office), after a VAO / Revenue Inspector enquiry.

faq.q: What does it cost and how long does it take?
faq.a: ₹60 e-Sevai service charge, typically 15–30 days.

state_pages.title: Legal Heir Certificate in Kerala — Portal, Documents, Fee & Timeline
state_pages.desc: How to get a legal-heir certificate in Kerala: Village Officer / Tahsildar, e-District Kerala, fee and timeline — including the 30-day objection period some guides describe.
state_pages.lede: In Kerala the legal-heir certificate is issued by the Tahsildar / Revenue Department after a Village Officer enquiry, through e-District Kerala.

sections.p: Apply on e-District Kerala or at the Village Office / Akshaya centre. A Village Officer enquiry follows the application.
₹2 stamp + ₹15 online; about ₹28 in total at an Akshaya centre.

sections.h: Timeline — two figures in the guides
sections.p: Most guides say 15–30 days. IndiaFilings and Housing.com describe a 30-day gazette objection period plus 15 days to issue after it — about 45 days in total. Both figures are shown here because the sources disagree.

faq.q: Who issues the legal-heir certificate in Kerala?
faq.a: The Tahsildar / Revenue Department, after a Village Officer enquiry.

faq.q: How long does it take?
faq.a: Most guides say 15–30 days. Some guides describe a 30-day objection period plus 15 days to issue (about 45 days).

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: ₹2 stamp + ₹15 online; about ₹28 in total at an Akshaya centre.

state_pages.title: Legal Heir Certificate in Karnataka — Restricted Issue, Seva Sindhu & the Succession Route
state_pages.desc: In Karnataka a legal-heir certificate is now only issued to the kin of deceased government servants. Everyone else needs a succession certificate from the civil court.
state_pages.lede: Karnataka is the restricted case: the Bengaluru Urban district page says a legal-heir certificate is now only issued to the kin of deceased government servants. Everyone else has to obtain a succession certificate through their jurisdictional civil court.

sections.p: Only the kin of a deceased government servant, for the deceased's service benefits. The portal is Seva Sindhu, and the timeline for these restricted cases is about 15 days (Seva Sindhu guides say 15–21 working days).

If the deceased was not a government servant, do not apply for a legal-heir certificate — apply for a succession certificate from the District Court instead. Nadakacheri covers family-tree and other revenue certificates, not a general legal-heir certificate.

faq.q: Can anyone get a legal-heir certificate in Karnataka?
faq.a: No. It is now only issued to the kin of deceased government servants, for service benefits.

faq.q: What should everyone else do?
faq.a: Obtain a succession certificate through the jurisdictional civil court.

faq.q: Which portal?
faq.a: Seva Sindhu (sevasindhu.karnataka.gov.in) for the restricted cases; Nadakacheri for family-tree / revenue certificates.

state_pages.title: Surviving Member Certificate (SMC) in Delhi — SDM, e-District, No Fee, 14 Days
state_pages.desc: Delhi does not issue a 'legal-heir certificate'. What it issues is a Surviving Member Certificate (SMC) from the SDM through Delhi e-District — no fee, 14 days.
state_pages.lede: Delhi does not issue a document called a 'legal-heir certificate'. What it issues is a Surviving Member Certificate (SMC) from the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM), Revenue Department, Government of NCT of Delhi — and that is what Delhi offices and banks mean when they ask for a legal-heir certificate.

sections.p: Apply online on Delhi e-District (edistrict.delhigovt.nic.in) or in person at the SDM's office. The certificate is issued by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM), Revenue Department, Government of NCT of Delhi.

The SMC lists the surviving members of the deceased. It identifies the heirs — Delhi offices and banks ask for it when they need proof of who the surviving family members are. It does not by itself authorise collecting bank deposits or shares: for that, banks usually ask for a succession certificate, or accept a nomination or indemnity depending on the amount and the bank's rules.

sections.h: SMC or succession certificate — which one?
sections.p: Delhi has two routes. The SMC from the SDM proves who the surviving members are. A succession certificate is a court order from the District Court under Sections 370–390 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, for collecting debts and securities such as bank deposits and shares. The court fee for a succession certificate in Delhi is 2.5% of the value of the debt or security in the certificate (Court Fees Act 1870 as amended for Delhi, Schedule I Article 12), and 4% on an extension under Section 376. No cap appears in the Article 12 text — one guide claims a Rs 3,00,000 cap, but that figure is not in the Act text, so confirm the fee with the District Court before filing. A succession certificate does not by itself transfer title to immovable property.
No fee is charged for the SMC. The certificate is issued in 14 days / 14 working days.

faq.q: Does Delhi issue a legal-heir certificate?
faq.a: Not by that name. Delhi issues a Surviving Member Certificate (SMC) through the SDM, Revenue Department.

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: No fee.

faq.q: How long does it take?
faq.a: 14 days / 14 working days.

faq.q: What is the SMC used for?
faq.a: It proves who the surviving members of the deceased are, for Delhi offices and banks that ask for a legal-heir certificate. It identifies the heirs; it does not by itself authorise collecting bank deposits or shares.

faq.q: Do I need an SMC or a succession certificate?
faq.a: An SMC if an office or bank asks for proof of the surviving members. A succession certificate from the District Court if you need to collect a debt or security, such as a bank deposit or shares.

faq.q: How much is the court fee for a succession certificate in Delhi?
faq.a: 2.5% of the value of the debt or security in the certificate (4% on an extension under Section 376). No cap appears in the Article 12 text, so confirm the fee with the District Court.

faq.q: Can I apply for the SMC online?
faq.a: Yes — on Delhi e-District (edistrict.delhigovt.nic.in), or in person at the SDM's office.

state_pages.title: Legal Heir Certificate in Maharashtra — Why There Isn't One, and the Heirship Certificate
state_pages.desc: Maharashtra has no notified 'legal-heir certificate' service. The equivalent is an heirship certificate under Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827, from the civil court.
state_pages.lede: Maharashtra has no notified 'legal-heir certificate' service — not in Mumbai and not anywhere else in the state. The equivalent is an heirship certificate under Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827, applied for in the civil court.

sections.p: Apply in the civil court (City Civil Court / Bombay High Court original side, by value) for an heirship certificate under Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827. The Maharashtra Court-Fees Act Sch.I Art.12 charges it at the probate rate on the property certified.
Use a succession certificate from the District Court instead — that is the route for bank deposits, shares, PF and insurance.

faq.q: Can I get a legal-heir certificate in Maharashtra?
faq.a: No — Maharashtra has no notified legal-heir certificate service.

faq.q: What is the alternative?
faq.a: An heirship certificate under Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827, from the civil court. For debts and securities, a succession certificate from the District Court.

timeline.detail: The first document — every later step needs it: the petition, the bank, the EPF claim, the insurance claim and the legal-heir application.

timeline.step: Identify the assets and all the heirs
timeline.detail: List every debt and security (for a succession certificate) and every legal heir — leaving one out can cause rejection. Check which assets have a nominee, because a nominee changes the route.

No will + need to collect debts/securities → succession certificate (court). Only need to prove who the heirs are (pension, mutation, small claims) → legal-heir certificate (revenue). Will exists → probate / letters of administration (voluntary since Dec 2025). All heirs agree on the division → a family settlement deed may avoid court.

timeline.step: File the petition and pay the court fee
timeline.detail: Petition under Section 372 before the District Judge where the deceased ordinarily resided (or where assets are). Pay the court fee on the schedule of debts/securities, via judicial stamp paper / deposit under Section 379.
The court issues notice to the heirs and publishes it in a newspaper (and in most states the official gazette) inviting objections.
Any person may file objections to the grant of the certificate.
Uncontested: a summary hearing on affidavit evidence, then the grant. Contested: a formal inquiry/trial with evidence and witnesses.
timeline.time: Grant often in months 2–4 if uncontested

timeline.detail: The court passes an order and issues the succession certificate.
timeline.time: Commonly 3–7 months uncontested (guides differ: 3–6, 4–7, 5–7, up to 12 months); contested cases take 1–3 years

_agree_notes.family_settlement: If every heir agrees on the division, a family settlement deed can record it without a court case — but banks and insurers may still ask for a succession certificate before releasing deposits or shares.
_agree_notes.no: If any legal heir objects, the petition becomes a contested case and will take much longer than the usual 3–6 months. Consider mediation or a family settlement first, and take legal advice before filing.
_agree_notes.unsure: Talk to all the legal heirs before filing. A succession petition needs the other heirs to either join or give NOC affidavits — an heir who is not told can object later and stall the case.

_law_notes.christian: For Christians and Parsis, succession is governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 itself. List all heirs under that Act.
_law_notes.hindu: Under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Class I heirs (spouse, children, mother, and others in the class) inherit together. The petition should list all of them, even if only one of them applies.
_law_notes.muslim: Under Muslim personal law, the heirs and their shares are fixed (sharers and residuaries), and they differ between the Sunni and Shia schools. List all heirs; a lawyer should confirm the shares for your school before filing.
_law_notes.other: Personal law decides who the legal heirs are. If you are not sure which law applies, a lawyer should confirm it before you file — the heir list in the petition must be right.

find_will.body: Whether you need a succession certificate or probate depends entirely on whether the deceased left a valid will. Check before you file anything: a succession certificate cannot be granted where a valid will exists (Section 370).
find_will.caveat: If a will turns up after a succession certificate is granted, tell the court — the position changes.
steps: Search the deceased's papers, bank locker (banks allow a locker search for a will), and any lawyer or CA the deceased used.
Ask the family — a will is often with the executor or a trusted family member.
Check if the will was registered at the sub-registrar's office.
Once you know, run this wizard again with the answer.
find_will.title: First step: find out whether there is a will

legal_heir.body: For government pension, gratuity and dues, the usual document is a legal-heir certificate from the Tahsildar / Revenue Department. It identifies who the legal heirs are. It is issued in many states — but not in all of them.
legal_heir.caveat: A legal-heir certificate identifies the heirs; it does not by itself authorise collecting bank deposits or shares.
steps: Check whether your state issues a legal-heir certificate (use the state finder on this site).
Apply on the state portal (e-District / e-Sevai / MeeSeva / Nadakacheri, depending on the state) or at the Tahsildar's office, with the death certificate, family details and the heirs' IDs.
A local inquiry (Talathi / Patwari / Village Officer) usually follows; the certificate is then issued, typically in 15–60 days depending on the state.
Use it for the pension, gratuity or dues claim. For bank deposits or shares, the bank may still ask for a succession certificate.
legal_heir.title: Your route: Legal-heir certificate — Tahsildar / Revenue Department

probate.body: The deceased left a valid will, so a succession certificate cannot be granted (Section 370 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925). The estate is dealt with under the will: probate, if the will names an executor, or letters of administration with the will annexed, if it does not. Since December 2025, probate is no longer a statutory precondition — Section 213 was omitted by the Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 (Act 37 of 2025; assent 20 Dec 2025, Gazette 21 Dec 2025) — but probate was NOT abolished: it remains available voluntarily, and banks and other institutions may still ask for it, especially for contested or high-value estates.
probate.caveat: This site does not publish a probate draft — the procedure depends on registration, the property's location and local court practice. A lawyer's help is worth it here.

links.text: Why we do not publish a probate draft →

steps: Find the original will — a copy is usually not enough for probate.
Check whether the will names an executor. If it does, the executor applies for probate; if not, an heir applies for letters of administration with the will annexed.

File in the court with jurisdiction over where the deceased lived or where the property is. Before December 2025, Section 213 made probate compulsory for some wills in Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; that section has been omitted, so probate is now voluntary — but a lawyer should confirm what the institution holding the asset requires.
The court issues notice to the heirs and publishes it; if nobody contests, probate is granted.
The executor/administrator then collects the assets and distributes them exactly as the will directs.
probate.title: Your route: Probate (or letters of administration) — not a succession certificate

property.body: For immovable property (house or land), a succession certificate does not transfer title. The usual route is: establish who the heirs are (legal-heir certificate where issued, or probate if there is a will), then apply for mutation of the property records in the heirs' names.
property.caveat: Mutation rules and stamp duty on family settlements vary by state — confirm at the sub-registrar's office.
steps: Get the death certificate and establish the heirs — legal-heir certificate from the Tahsildar where your state issues one; probate if there is a will.
Apply for mutation of the property records (municipal / revenue records) with the death certificate, the heir document, and the property papers.
If the property is to be sold, the buyer and the sub-registrar will usually want the mutation done (or probate, if there is a will).
If all heirs agree, a family settlement deed can record how the property is divided — it must be registered if it deals with immovable property.
property.title: Your route: Legal-heir certificate + mutation — not a succession certificate

succession.body: There is no will, and the assets are debts or securities (bank deposits, shares, PF, insurance). A succession certificate from the District Court is the usual route: it authorises the heirs to collect the deceased person's debts and securities.
succession.caveat: A succession certificate does not transfer title to immovable property.
steps: Get the death certificate first — every step after this needs it.

List every debt and security (bank accounts, FDs, shares/Demat, PF, insurance) with approximate values — the certificate covers only what is listed in the petition. Check which assets have a nominee: with a nominee, banks must not insist on a succession certificate (RBI Directions, 2025).
Get NOC affidavits from the other legal heirs (use the NOC generator on this site).
File a petition under Section 372 before the District Judge where the deceased ordinarily resided, with the court fee for your state.

The court publishes a notice (about 45 days — some guides say 30–45 days) for objections. If nobody objects, the court grants the certificate — commonly 3–7 months for an uncontested case (guides differ: 3–6, 4–7, 5–7 and up to 12 months).
succession.title: Your route: Succession certificate — District Court, Section 372
